prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

For James Welch The first harvest of wheat in flatlands along the Milk startled me into thoughts of you and this place we both remember and also forget as home. Maybe it was the familiarity or maybe it was my own need to ask if you have ever regretted leaving. What bends, what gives? And have you ever missed this wind?—it has now grown warm with late summer, but soon it will be as dangerous as the bobcat stalking calves and pets just south of the river. Men take out their dogs, a case of beer and wait in their pickups for dawn, for a chance with their rifles. They don’t understand that she isn’t going to make any mistakes. With winter my need for an answer grows more desperate and there are only four roads out. One is the same cat hunters drive with mannish glory and return along, gun still oil-shined and unshot. Another goes deeper into Assiniboine territory: This is the one I should talk myself into taking next. I haven’t much traveled the third except to visit a hospital where, after the first time, my mother had refused chemotherapy. And the last road you know as well as I do— past the coral-painted Catholic church, its doors long ago sealed shut to the mouth of Mission Canyon, then south just a ways, to where the Rockies cut open and forgive. There you and I are on the ascent. After that, the arrival is what matters most.

outputs.L2:
For James Welch

The season’s first wheat cutting on the plains beside the Milk brought you suddenly to mind, along with this place that both of us claim as home and, in other ways, fail to remember as one. Perhaps it was because everything felt so known, or perhaps because I needed to wonder whether you have ever felt sorry for going away. What yields, and what breaks? Do you ever long for this wind? By now it has turned warm in the late-summer air, though before long it will become as threatening as the bobcat hunting calves and household animals south of the river. Men bring their dogs and a case of beer, sitting in their trucks until daybreak, hoping for a shot. They do not realize she will not slip up.

When winter comes, my hunger for a reply becomes more urgent, and there are only four ways out. One road is the same one the cat hunters take in their hard, swaggering pride, then follow back again with their rifles still glossy with oil and never fired. A second road leads farther into Assiniboine country; that is the route I ought to persuade myself to choose next. I have hardly taken the third, except to go to a hospital where my mother, after the first visit, would not accept chemotherapy. The fourth road is one you know just as well as I do: it passes the Catholic church painted coral, its doors sealed shut long ago, and runs on to the mouth of Mission Canyon, then a little farther south, to the place where the Rockies open themselves and grant pardon. There, you and I are climbing. Beyond that, what matters most is reaching the destination.
outputs.L3:
The first wheat harvest along the Milk River brings James Welch to the speaker’s mind, along with the complicated idea of home that they seem to share. The landscape is not simply a backdrop but a place filled with memory, attachment, and unease. It carries the weight of belonging, yet also the pressure that can make departure feel necessary. In remembering Welch, the speaker recognizes a bond shaped by the same country, the same wind, and the same difficult pull between staying and leaving.

This reflection leads to questions about regret. The speaker wonders what it means to leave home behind and whether such a choice can ever be made cleanly. Even after departure, certain details remain vivid: the wind moving across the plains, the wide fields, the river, and the familiar distances of the land. The speaker asks whether these remembered elements are missed, whether they return in memory as comfort or as accusation. Home becomes both a physical place and an emotional burden, something one may escape but never entirely lose.

The text also contrasts human confidence with the quiet intelligence of the natural world. Hunters wait for a bobcat, carrying with them a sense of bravado and expectation. They imagine themselves prepared, skilled, and in control. Yet the bobcat represents another kind of mastery: instinctive, silent, and elusive. Its ability to remain unseen and to move according to its own logic challenges human certainty. Against the animal’s natural skill, human bravado appears fragile, even foolish.

As winter deepens, the speaker’s longing for answers becomes more urgent. The cold season sharpens the sense of isolation and turns reflection into a search for direction. This search is imagined through four possible roads leading away from the place. Each road suggests a different form of departure, a different way of asking what lies beyond home and what might be gained or lost by leaving it. The roads become symbols of choice, memory, and the desire for meaning.

The final road carries the speaker past familiar landmarks and toward the Rocky Mountains. This movement is not merely geographical; it becomes a journey toward clarity. The known world gives way to elevation, distance, and the promise of arrival. In the Rockies, ascent itself becomes meaningful. To climb is to move beyond uncertainty, to seek perspective, and to approach a destination that is both physical and spiritual. By the end, the road’s importance lies not only in where it leads, but in the act of rising toward something larger than the place left behind.
outputs.L4:
The speaker addresses James Welch directly, using that address as a way to think through the meaning of home in the Milk River flatlands. The landscape is not presented as a simple place of comfort or origin; it is a place layered with memory, weather, violence, departure, and desire. As the speaker moves through recollections of the region, the flatlands become both real and symbolic: a physical home marked by roads, seasons, and distances, and an emotional territory shaped by longing and loss.

The poem traces the Milk River country through changes in season and atmosphere. The land appears under different lights and conditions, suggesting that memory itself is always shifting. Winter, summer, darkness, wind, and open space all become part of how the speaker understands the place. These details keep the landscape from becoming merely nostalgic. It is beautiful, but it is also harsh; it holds belonging, but it also contains pain. The speaker remembers not only the land’s quietness and distance, but also its history of local violence and human damage. Home, in this poem, is therefore complicated: it is loved, but it is not innocent.

The image of four roads leading outward becomes central to the speaker’s meditation. Each road suggests a possible departure, a way to leave the flatlands behind and move toward another life. Yet the roads do not offer simple freedom. To leave home is also to carry it along in memory, and to return is not necessarily to recover what has been lost. The poem holds escape and return in tension, refusing to decide whether one is better or more truthful than the other. The speaker seems to understand that longing can exist in both directions: one may long to get away, and later long just as strongly to come back.

Among these roads, the remembered road toward the Rocky Mountains becomes especially important. Unlike the other roads, it offers a sense of rising, of moving upward from the flatlands toward a larger and more forgiving horizon. This ascent does not erase the difficulty of the past, but it briefly transforms it. The movement toward the mountains suggests the possibility of release, perspective, and forgiveness. In that moment, the poem discovers a form of arrival that is not simply geographical. To arrive is not only to reach a destination; it is to recognize the depth of one’s attachment to a place, even after leaving it.

Ultimately, the poem does not resolve the speaker’s divided feelings about home. The desire to depart and the desire to return remain intertwined. What endures is the remembered landscape itself: the Milk River flatlands, the roads leading away, the violence and tenderness held in memory, and the distant promise of the Rockies. Through these images, the poem suggests that belonging is measured less by staying or leaving than by the intensity with which a place continues to live inside the mind. Arrival, then, becomes the deepest form of belonging—not because it ends longing, but because it reveals how fully the speaker has been shaped by the place remembered.
outputs.L5:
For readers discovering contemporary Native American literature, James Welch remains an essential figure. Born in 1940, Welch was a writer of Blackfeet and Gros Ventre heritage whose novels and poetry helped bring Indigenous voices into wider American literary discussions.

James Welch is best known for works such as *Winter in the Blood*, *The Death of Jim Loney*, and *Fools Crow*. His writing often explores identity, displacement, cultural memory, and the lasting effects of colonial history. Rather than presenting simplified portraits, Welch created complex characters who struggle with belonging, family, tradition, and the modern world.

For many scholars and readers, Welch’s greatest achievement is his ability to combine quiet, lyrical language with deep emotional power. His work does not rely on easy answers. Instead, it invites reflection on history, survival, and the meaning of home. Through his novels and poems, James Welch helped shape a lasting literary legacy and opened doors for future generations of Indigenous writers.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem titled “For James Welch” set in Montana’s Milk River country, reflecting on home, leaving, winter, roads, Assiniboine territory, and the Rockies.
counterfactuals.output:
## For James Welch

In the Milk River country, winter learns the names of everything by covering it. The coulees, the chokecherry brush, the fence posts leaning like old men in their sleep, the two-lane road going white at the shoulders and black in the middle where the tires keep faith. Snow comes down without hurry, as if it has always been coming down, as if the sky were only remembering how to return to earth.

This is home, or one of the words for home: a house lit low against the weather, a dog’s track vanishing toward the cottonwoods, the river under ice carrying its dark sentence east. Home is the smell of wool thawing by the stove, coffee gone bitter in the pot, a pickup ticking in the yard. Home is also the thing you leave because the road keeps talking, because there are towns beyond the next rise, and beyond them other towns, each with its bar mirror, its motel window, its neon trembling in the cold.

We were always leaving, even when we stayed. Leaving in our thoughts, in our worn boots by the door, in the maps folded beneath the seat. The highway ran through Assiniboine territory like a scar that had learned to shine. It carried wheat trucks, school buses, soldiers, cousins, strangers, men with their collars up against the wind. It carried all that had been taken and all that could not be taken: names held in the mouth, stories buried and waking, the old presence of the people moving with the weather across grass gone silver with frost.

Out west, the Rockies stood blue and unreachable, shouldering the last light. They were not a promise, exactly, but they made promise possible. At evening they gathered the sun in their ravines and gave back a cold fire. We looked toward them and felt the distance inside us open—felt how a life could be measured by roads, by departures, by the long ache of returning to a place that has changed and has not changed, where the wind knows you before anyone speaks.

And the Milk River kept on, narrow and stubborn under its lid of ice, winding through the breaks as though it remembered a warmer world. Above it, the stars came out hard and bright. Below them, the land lay vast, intimate, unfinished. If you listened, you could hear winter breathing through the grass, hear tires far off on the highway, hear the old country speaking in snow and stone and silence: You can go, it said. You can go a long way. But some roads are made of memory, and they bring you back in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an intimate, elegiac paragraph addressed to James Welch in the style of contemporary Native American lyric nonfiction, with imagery of wheat harvest, bobcats, hunters, a Catholic church, Mission Canyon, and four roads out.
counterfactuals.output: James, I keep looking for you where the wheat is cut low and gold dust lifts from the combines like a last breath, where bobcats cross the ditch at dusk with the old, unhurried knowledge of survivors, and hunters come down from the breaks carrying their rifles as if they have also carried grief too long. I want to tell you the Catholic church is still there in my mind, its bell a dark bead on the tongue, its saints watching the reservation road with chipped eyes, while beyond it Mission Canyon opens and closes like a wound the weather keeps touching. You taught us how the dead stay near—not as ghosts exactly, but as wind in grass, as hunger, as the story that refuses the museum case and walks home alone. Tonight there are four roads out, each pale with distance, each promising another country and returning me to this one: the road of blood, the road of snow, the road of names nearly lost, the road where your voice goes on ahead, quiet and broken and beautiful, asking us to listen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic letter beginning “For James Welch” that meditates on memory, exile, regret, and returning home to the flatlands along the Milk River.
counterfactuals.output:
For James Welch,

I write from a room that has forgotten the wind,  
from a city where the streets shine after rain  
but never smell of sage, or mud, or cattle,  
or the iron sweetness of water moving slow.

Memory is not a house.  
It has no door one can open gently,  
no lamp left burning in the window.  
It is more like the Milk River in thaw,  
brown and shouldering its way through the flats,  
carrying fence posts, willow limbs,  
the names of those who went under  
and those who merely went away.

I have been away so long  
that regret has learned to speak in my voice.  
It says: you should have stayed  
when the cottonwoods were leafing out;  
you should have listened longer  
to the old ones at the table,  
their stories bending like grass  
under a weather no map could name.  
It says: you left before you knew  
what leaving was.

Exile begins quietly.  
Not with a train, not with the road,  
not with the last look back at the grain elevator  
or the dogs lifting their heads in the yard,  
but later—years later—  
when you wake before dawn  
and cannot remember the exact color  
of your father’s hands,  
or the sound of meadowlarks  
rising out of the ditch grass,  
or the shape of your own shadow  
on a road without trees.

Still, the flatlands keep their counsel.  
They do not forgive easily,  
but they remember without ceremony.  
The coulees hold their dark.  
The river bends where it has always bent.  
Dust moves over the section lines  
like a thought returning to its source.

If I came home now,  
would the land know me?  
Would it take one look  
at my polished shoes, my careful grief,  
and turn its face away?  
Or would it say nothing,  
which is the truest welcome—  
the sky widening above me,  
the river dragging its old mirror  
through the willows,  
the prairie opening its long, unsentimental arms?

I have carried home inside me  
like a stone in the mouth:  
hard, necessary, unsayable.  
Tonight I set it down on the table.  
Tonight I let the wind come in.  
I let it scatter the papers,  
lift the curtains,  
cross the miles of wheat and winter pasture  
until it reaches the Milk River,  
where everything lost  
is still traveling,  
and everything that returns  
arrives changed,  
but arrives.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense literary passage inspired by James Welch, blending Montana landscape, Indigenous place, family illness, rural violence, and a final movement toward the Rocky Mountains.
counterfactuals.output:
By late August the grass had gone the color of old rope and the coulees north of the agency held their heat like iron kettles. All day the wind worried the tin roof of my mother’s house, lifting one corner with a complaint that sounded almost human, and in the bedroom where the shades were drawn against the white violence of noon, my uncle breathed in his narrow bed as if he were hauling something heavy up from the bottom of a creek. The women came and went with jars of chokecherry syrup, soup gone thin in the pot, pills counted into saucers. They spoke softly in the kitchen, but their voices traveled through the walls with the smell of coffee and Lysol, with the dust of the road and the sweet rot of cottonwoods along the river.

Outside, the country lay open and pitiless, but never empty. The buttes stood blue in the distance, notched and shouldered, and every draw had a name older than the survey stakes, older than the cattle fences sagging into sage. There was a place where the people said a woman had hidden from soldiers with her baby under a bank of clay; there was a ridge where the old men had watched the buffalo go down like weather. We passed these places without speaking, as if speech might disturb what remained there—bone, story, breath, the stubborn grasses coming back each spring from their burned crowns.

My brother arrived at dusk in a borrowed pickup with one headlight and blood on his cuff. He said it was deer blood, then said nothing. Behind him the sun went down red over the stubble fields and the yard dogs began to bark at the empty road. Later we heard how a man from town had been found near the stock pond, beaten with a tire iron after cards and whiskey and some old insult pulled up by the roots. In that country violence did not arrive like a stranger; it sat at the table, wore somebody’s hat, knew the way to every house. My mother closed her eyes when the sheriff’s cruiser rolled past slow, its lights unlit, and my uncle, who had not spoken for two days, turned his face to the wall.

Night came cold. The stars broke out hard and near, and the wind moved over the prairie with the long, dry sound of a dress dragging through weeds. I stood by the fence and looked west, beyond the dark backs of the horses, beyond the grain elevators and the towns with their bars glowing weakly in the blue distance. There, where the world lifted at last into stone, the Rocky Mountains held the last light like a promise no one had earned. In the morning, I knew, we would drive toward them—past the mission, past the cutbanks, past the fields gone silver with frost—carrying my uncle’s silence, my brother’s trouble, my mother’s prayers, and all that vast, broken country rising ahead of us, mountain by mountain, into the cold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem in second person addressed to a remembered writer, using late-summer harvest, dangerous winter wind, hunters in pickups, Assiniboine land, a mother refusing chemotherapy, and a sealed Catholic church as key images.
counterfactuals.output:
You are still there at the edge of late summer, where the fields give themselves up in gold sheets and the combines move slowly as weather, taking the heads from wheat, taking the sun down with them. I remember you in that harvest light, your notebook closed on the dashboard, your face turned toward the Assiniboine land as if listening were a form of apology. The grass had gone brittle. The chokecherries were darkening. Everywhere the world seemed to be storing sweetness against what it knew would come.

You told me once that winter here did not arrive but escaped—through coulees, across frozen sloughs, over the open roads with a blade in its mouth. A dangerous wind, you said, could make a person religious or cruel. Later, when the hunters passed in pickups before dawn, rifles racked in the back windows, coffee steaming between their knees, their headlights crossing the ditches like search parties, I thought of how you had written them without judgment: men in caps and orange vests, driving into the first hard weather, looking for the living thing that would make them feel alive.

Your mother refused chemotherapy in the same plain voice she used to refuse second helpings. No, she said, and the word stood in the kitchen like a black post. Outside, the garden was collapsing into its own abundance: tomatoes splitting, squash hardening under the leaves, the last beans hanging like small green questions. You watched her turn away from the doctors’ language, from the bright rooms and their mercies, and you did not call it courage, though others did. You let it remain what it was: a woman closing the gate to her body.

Now the Catholic church is sealed, its doors chained, its windows clouded with dust and old breath. No bell. No votive flame. No one crossing themselves in the vestibule with fingers smelling of soil and diesel. The saints are locked inside with their painted wounds, and snow gathers where the parish women once stamped their boots. You would have noticed the notice taped to the door, the official seal, the way abandonment can look almost ceremonial.

I speak to you because memory is also a country, and you left tracks through mine: stubble fields, gravel roads, the wind sharpening itself on fence wire, the dead carried not upward but inward. You taught me that a place is never empty, not even when the church is closed, not even when the house goes quiet after the mother dies, not even when the hunters come home with blood in the truck bed and dusk in their eyes. Late summer keeps returning with its arms full. Winter keeps waiting beyond the hill. And you, remembered writer, keep walking ahead of me through the cut fields, touching nothing, naming everything.
